title.en: Derive the output of an op-amp integrator
Derive the output of an op-amp differentiator
Explain the comparator and zero-crossing detector

say.en: Swap a resistor for a capacitor and the op-amp starts doing calculus: it integrates or differentiates the input. Remove the feedback and it simply compares two voltages. In this lesson: Derive the output of an op-amp integrator.
Derive the output of an op-amp differentiator.
Explain the comparator and zero-crossing detector.

body.en: In the *integrator*, the input is applied through R and a capacitor C is the feedback element. At the virtual ground the input current $V_i/R$ charges C: $V_i/R = -C\,dV_o/dt$, so $V_o = -\dfrac{1}{RC}\int V_i\,dt$. A constant input gives a linear ramp of slope $-V_i/RC$; a square wave becomes a triangular wave. In practice a large resistor is placed across C to stop the output drifting into saturation at very low frequencies.

narration.en: The integrator has R at the input and C in the feedback. Its output is minus one over RC times the integral of the input, so a square wave becomes a triangle.
narration.kn: ಇಂಟಿಗ್ರೇಟರ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿ ಇನ್‌ಪುಟ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿ R, ಪ್ರತಿಪೋಷಣೆಯಲ್ಲಿ C. ಔಟ್‌ಪುಟ್ = −(1/RC)∫Vi dt; ಚೌಕ ತರಂಗ ತ್ರಿಕೋನ ತರಂಗವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

say.en: Put a capacitor in the feedback path and a resistor at the input. The output becomes minus one over RC times the integral of the input.
A steady input gives a steady ramp, so a square wave becomes a triangular wave.
Swap R and C and you get a differentiator. Remove the feedback altogether and the op-amp becomes a comparator.

body.en: In the *differentiator* the positions are swapped: C at the input and R in the feedback. The capacitor current $C\,dV_i/dt$ flows through R, so $V_o = -RC\,dV_i/dt$. A triangular wave becomes a square wave and a sine becomes a (negative) cosine whose amplitude grows with frequency, $2\pi f RC V_m$. A comparator uses the op-amp without feedback: because the gain is huge, the output goes to $+V_{sat}$ when $V_+ > V_-$ and to $-V_{sat}$ when $V_+ < V_-$. With one input grounded it is a zero-crossing detector that turns a sine wave into a square wave.

narration.en: The differentiator has C at the input and R in the feedback, so its output is minus RC times the rate of change of the input. A comparator has no feedback and swings to plus or minus saturation.

problem.en: An integrator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 1 µF. A steady +1 V is applied at t = 0 with the output at 0 V. Find Vo after 50 ms, and when it saturates (Vsat = ±13 V).

steps.en: It reaches −13 V at t = 13/100 = 0.13 s = 130 ms.

narration.en: Let us work this out together. An integrator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 1 µF. A steady +1 V is applied at t = 0 with the output at 0 V. Find Vo after 50 ms, and when it saturates (Vsat = ±13 V).

say.en: Let us work this out together. An integrator has R equals 10 k ohms and C equals 1 microfarad. A steady plus 1 volt is applied at t equals 0 with the output at 0 volts. Find Vo after 50 milliseconds, and when it saturates (Vsat equals plus or minus 13 volts).
RC equals 10 to the power 4 times 10 to the power minus 6 equals 0.01 seconds equals 10 milliseconds.
Slope equals -Vi over RC equals minus 1 over 0.01 equals minus 100 volts per second.
After 50 milliseconds: Vo equals minus 100 times 0.05 equals minus 5 volts.
It reaches minus 13 volts at t equals 13 over 100 equals 0.13 seconds equals 130 milliseconds.
So the answer is minus 5 volts; saturates after 130 milliseconds.

problem.en: A differentiator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF. Find the output amplitude for a 1 V peak, 1 kHz sine input.

steps.en: Vo = −RC × d(sin 2πft)/dt has amplitude 2πf RC Vm.

narration.en: Let us work this out together. A differentiator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF. Find the output amplitude for a 1 V peak, 1 kHz sine input.

say.en: Let us work this out together. A differentiator has R equals 10 k ohms and C equals 0.1 microfarads. Find the output amplitude for a 1 volt peak, 1 kilohertz sine input.
RC equals 10 to the power 4 times 10 to the power minus 7 equals 10 to the power minus 3 seconds.
Vo equals -RC times dsin 2 pi ft/dt has amplitude 2 pi f RC Vm.
Amplitude equals 2 pi times 1000 times 10 to the power minus 3 times 1 equals 6.28 volts a negative cosine.
So the answer is About 6.28 volts peak.
